\chapter{Courtesy Words}
\label{ch:hi-courtesy}
\hlchaptermodality{50}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can thank someone in Hindi at the weight the occasion asks for.}

\section[ābhār]{\hi{आभार} (ābhār) — gratitude}

\label{lesson:HI-C50-gratitude}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{nikalnā} mean, and what did \emph{mulāqāt} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आभार}}
\textbf{\hi{आभार}} (\emph{ābhār}) — \textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{ā-bhāra}, 'a load carried toward' — built on \emph{bhṛ-}, 'to bear', which is the same ancient root as Latin \emph{ferre} and English \textquotedblleft{}bear\textquotedblright{}. To be grateful, on the evidence of this word, is to be carrying a weight that somebody else put there.

It stands above \hi{धन्यवाद} in formality, and well above \hi{शुक्रिया}. It is the word a written speech uses, or a letter, or the last line of a printed programme.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five courtesy words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ābhār}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ābhār}, then \emph{mulāqāt}, the thanks and the meeting it ends
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{आभार} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ehsān]{\hi{एहसान} (ehsān) — a favour}

\label{lesson:HI-C50-favour}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ābhār} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{एहसान}}
\textbf{\hi{एहसान}} (\emph{ehsān}) — \textquotedblleft{}a favour\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{iḥsān}, 'the doing of what is good', on the root \emph{ḥ-s-n}, which carries both beauty and goodness and also gives the names \emph{ḥasan} and \emph{ḥusn}. Persian passed it on to Hindi as the word for a kindness done to you and not forgotten.

Two phrases live on it and point opposite ways. \emph{Ehsān mānnā} is to acknowledge a favour; \emph{ehsān jatānā} is to keep reminding somebody that you did them one. The language leaves you in no doubt which of the two it thinks less of.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: gratitude, and the thing it is owed for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ehsān}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ehsān}, then \emph{ābhār}, the favour and the thanks for it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{एहसान} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a favour\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ādar]{\hi{आदर} (ādar) — respect}

\label{lesson:HI-C50-respect}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ehsān} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आदर}}
\textbf{\hi{आदर}} (\emph{ādar}) — \textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{ādara}, 'regard, attentiveness', from \emph{ā-dṛ-}, 'to heed'. Hindi carries this word inside its own machinery: the \hi{आप} form is called \emph{ādar-sūcak}, the respect-marking form.

So this is not only a word for a feeling somebody has. It is the name of a choice the language makes you make in nearly every sentence you speak, whether you have thought about it or not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one is built into the grammar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ādar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ādar}, then \emph{ehsān}, then \emph{ābhār}, back down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{आदर} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āśīrvād]{\hi{आशीर्वाद} (āśīrvād) — a blessing}

\label{lesson:HI-C50-blessing}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ādar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आशीर्वाद}}
\textbf{\hi{आशीर्वाद}} (\emph{āśīrvād}) — \textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{āśīr-vāda}: \emph{āśis}, 'a wish, a prayer', joined to \emph{vāda}, 'speech'. A blessing is literally a wish said out loud. The \emph{s} turning into \emph{r} before the \emph{v} is a regular joint in Sanskrit rather than a quirk of this one word.

It travels downward. An elder gives \hi{आशीर्वाद}; the younger person asks for it by bending to touch the elder's feet, and the giving is spoken over the bent head.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is given rather than said.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āśīrvād}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āśīrvād}, then \emph{ādar}, the blessing and the respect that asks for it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{आशीर्वाद} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[praṇām]{\hi{प्रणाम} (praṇām) — a bow, a salutation}

\label{lesson:HI-C50-salutation}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{āśīrvād} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{प्रणाम}}
\textbf{\hi{प्रणाम}} (\emph{praṇām}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bow, a salutation\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{pra-ṇāma}, 'a bending forward', on \emph{nam-}, 'to bow' — the identical root standing inside \hi{नमस्ते} and \hi{नमस्कार}. Three words, one gesture, three heights of formality.

\hi{प्रणाम} is what a younger person says to an elder, often while bending to touch the feet, and what it expects back is \hi{आशीर्वाद}. The pair of words is the pair of movements: one goes down, one comes back over the top.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: gratitude, a favour, respect, a blessing, a bow.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{praṇām}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{ābhār}, \emph{ehsān}, \emph{ādar}, \emph{āśīrvād}, \emph{praṇām}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{प्रणाम} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bow, a salutation\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
